title: Perimeter Protocol
protagonist: Marcus Webb, Security Operations Analyst, regional hospital network IT security desk
primary_metric: true threats blocked per false positive generated

options.A: Approve Rule Set A ("Broad Net") — block if p OR q (disjunction): watchlist hit OR unpatched-port hit, catching more real threats but generating more false positives
options.B: Approve Rule Set B ("Narrow Gate") — block only if p AND q (conjunction): watchlist hit AND unpatched-port hit, generating far fewer false positives but letting more real threats through

deliverables.text: Two complete truth tables: Rule Set A's block condition (p OR q) and Rule Set B's block condition (p AND q), all four rows each, every output labeled True/False.
A worked classification table applying both truth tables to the Traffic Sample (Appendix C): true threats blocked and false positives generated under each rule set.
A negation exercise: negate p, negate q, negate Rule Set A's full block condition, and identify which Traffic Sample requests satisfy the negation.
A converse/inverse/contrapositive analysis of the watchlist conditional statement, tested against the Traffic Sample, naming which of the four statements Rule Set B implicitly relies on.
A false-positive-cost comparison using the D2 totals and the per-alert triage cost, producing each rule set's true-threats-blocked-per-false-positive ratio and the margin between them.

balance.argument_a: Rule Set A (disjunction) blocks every threat Rule Set B blocks, plus more -- on the 20-request Traffic Sample it blocks 10 of the 11 genuine threats present, missing only 1, versus Rule Set B's 4 of 11. In raw threats-caught terms A is more than double B, and A's total weekend triage time (6 false positives x 15 minutes = 90 minutes) is still a small fraction of the 20-hour skeleton-crew pool.
balance.argument_b: Rule Set B (conjunction) generates far fewer false positives (2 versus A's 6 on the sample) and comes out ahead on the case's own stated primary metric -- true threats blocked per false positive -- because its narrow trigger condition keeps its false-positive denominator small even though its true-positive numerator is smaller too. It also uses a smaller share of the fixed weekend analyst-hour pool (30 minutes versus A's 90).
balance.margin_basis: Compare true-threats-blocked-per-false-positive (the stated primary metric) for Rule Set A vs. Rule Set B, computed from the D2 classification counts once the Traffic Sample (Appendix C) is classified under each rule set's truth table (D1).

modeling_assumptions.statement: The weekend skeleton crew has a fixed analyst-hour pool for alert triage.
modeling_assumptions.basis: Stated scenario constraint sized for a small two-person weekend on-call crew; no public per-hospital SOC staffing figure exists.

modeling_assumptions.statement: The Weekend Traffic Sample (Table C-1) is a hand-built 20-request stand-in for the deployment weekend's inbound traffic.
modeling_assumptions.value_used: 20 requests, with p, q, and ground-truth-threat flags set as shown in Table C-1
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public per-hospital firewall log exists or should exist; built by hand to keep the mix of watchlist-only, unpatched-port-only, both, and neither traffic internally consistent and gradable, following the same stated-scenario pattern as grant-reach's 9,000-student population.

modeling_assumptions.statement: Average analyst time to triage one false-positive alert.
modeling_assumptions.basis: No clean per-alert figure is published; anchored to two real Ponemon Institute surveys (S2, S3) establishing that false-positive triage consumes a large, real share of analyst time and real six-to-seven-figure annual costs for a full organization, without literally transferring either survey's own rate or annual total.

sensitivity_note: Hospital/clinical framing touches infrastructure protecting patient care (SPEC §6). Keep the case about the access-control decision only — never about a specific breach's harm to patients, no named real hospital, no real incident. Routine administrative security math, comparable in register to Key Length or Codebreaker.

cohort_bands.note: Run the full anchor ladder. Split into two desks for D1/D2 (one desk builds Rule Set A's truth table and classification, the other Rule Set B's) before reconvening to compare totals — this mirrors the real workflow of two analysts dividing the two rule sets.

Skip the desk split — build both truth tables together on the board, then split only for D2's classification pass (half the group classifies under Rule Set A, half under Rule Set B) before merging results.
Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position, not a cold-call vote. The facilitator argues the opposite rule set directly. Both truth tables are still built individually before comparing.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The count of genuine threats among p-AND-q traffic (Table C-1 rows 1-6) is part of the hand-built Traffic Sample (MA2) -- no real per-hospital firewall log exists or could be published, so the true mix for any actual weekend's traffic is an irreducible unknown, not something research could pin down. A -50% flex flips the winner to Rule Set A; a +50% flex pushes the margin to 50.0%, past the SPEC S2 20% cap.

The count of false positives among p-AND-q traffic is likewise part of the hand-built MA2 sample. A +50% flex flips the winner to Rule Set A (margin 7.1%); a -50% flex pushes the margin to 100.0%, far past the 20% cap in Rule Set B's favor.
The count of genuine threats among watchlist-only (p AND NOT q) traffic is part of MA2. A -50% flex pushes the margin to 41.2%, past the SPEC S2 cap, without flipping the winner.
The count of false positives among watchlist-only traffic is part of MA2. A -50% flex ties the two rule sets exactly (margin 0%); a +50% flex pushes the margin to 40.0%, past the cap.
The count of genuine threats among unpatched-port-only (NOT p AND q) traffic is part of MA2. A -50% flex pushes the margin to 41.2%, past the SPEC S2 cap, without flipping the winner.
The count of false positives among unpatched-port-only traffic is part of MA2. A -50% flex ties the two rule sets exactly (margin 0%); a +50% flex pushes the margin to 40.0%, past the cap.
